title: Linux Advanced Administration
description: Learn advanced Linux commands for process management, file permissions, ownership modification, network testing, and logs inspection.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with procps installed and the usual /proc visibility, use ps to take a detailed snapshot of all current processes, including their user identity and command line.
tasks.explanation: ps aux selects processes with and without terminals and gives user-oriented detail, including user identity and command line. ps -ef provides an alternative full listing. ps is a snapshot; interactive monitors update continuously.

tasks.prompt: In Ubuntu Bash, a process you own has PID 1234. Use the kill builtin to forcefully terminate that process with SIGKILL (signal 9).
tasks.explanation: -9 selects SIGKILL and 1234 is the sole target PID. Unlike SIGTERM, SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored and offers no cleanup opportunity. You can signal your own process without sudo; 'kill 9 1234' instead targets two PIDs with the default signal.

tasks.prompt: In your Ubuntu home directory, you own the regular file script.sh with no extended ACL. Use chmod with octal notation to set owner read/write/execute, group and others read/execute, and no special bits (755).
tasks.hint: Use chmod command with octal 755: 'chmod 755 script.sh'
tasks.explanation: 'chmod 755' assigns full permissions (7) to the owner, and read/execute (5) to the group and others.

tasks.prompt: As an ordinary Ubuntu user with sudo access, use chown to change both owner and group of the existing file.txt in your home directory to root.
tasks.explanation: chown uses owner:group to change both identities. sudo is required to transfer ownership to root; changing only the owner would leave the group unchanged.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with iputils ping installed and configured for ordinary-user ICMP requests, use ping to send exactly four IPv4 echo requests to 8.8.8.8.
tasks.explanation: ping -c 4 sends four ICMP echo requests and then stops. Replies can demonstrate IP reachability, but their absence may also mean filtering rather than a host failure.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with systemd, you have sudo access but no direct permission to read the full system journal. Use journalctl to follow new entries in that journal in real time.
tasks.explanation: journalctl -f displays recent journal entries and waits for new ones. sudo grants access to the full system journal; tailing a text syslog file reads a different log source.
